behaviours.name: Developing your craft
behaviours.def: How you learn, develop, and grow the capability of those around you. Covers self-awareness, seeking and applying feedback, and knowledge sharing.

levels.6: Graduate:
• You are aware of the areas of your practice you are capable in, and those where you need to build further capability.

• You seek specific feedback close to the activity, asking 'what did I do well in this' and 'what can I improve'.

• You focus on developing the core skills needed to deliver your craft, applying feedback to adjust your approach on live work.
levels.7: Junior:
• You are aware of the areas of your practice you are capable in, and those where you need to build further capability.

• You seek specific feedback close to the activity, asking 'what did I do well in this' and 'what can I improve'.

• You focus on developing the core skills needed to deliver your craft, applying feedback to adjust your approach on live work.
levels.8: Mid:
• You identify appropriate sources of guidance to inform your development needs and pursue opportunities to build your skills and experience.

• You seek targeted feedback from those around you to develop your craft, and make use of the learning opportunities available to you.

• You contribute to knowledge sharing by passing on what you have learnt from your work so others can benefit from it.

• You learn new skills needed for upcoming projects and proactively discuss these with your line manager or project lead.
levels.9: Senior:
• You take ownership for your own development, seeking targeted feedback and input from others to sharpen your craft.

• You have a clear view of your gaps and actively learn from colleagues with strengths in those areas.

• You make your learnings and craft visible to others, sharing your work and your thinking openly so colleagues know where to bring you in.

• You deepen the knowledge of others by promoting good practice and sharing the latest thinking with others in your practice area.
levels.10: Lead:
• You take ownership for your development, contribute towards the development of others, and actively learn from more senior colleagues to address your own gaps.

• You understand how your working style influences those around you and demonstrate the learning behaviours you expect in others, taking on feedback from less senior colleagues.

• You demonstrate good practice in your area through how you create approaches that others can follow and bring new ideas into your work to keep the practice current.

• You introduce new approaches into your work and share these with others in your practice area.
levels.11: Principal:
• You model effective learning across projects you're working on. You're aware of how your approach and behaviour shape those around you.

• You treat projects as opportunities for learning, innovation, and development, ensuring colleagues actively contribute to continuous improvement of our practices and approaches.

• You shape the development of others at scale, drawing on your significant domain expertise to inform their plans and pathways.

• You evolve the practice by bringing emerging and innovative approaches into how your practice area works.
levels.12: Head of:
• You set the direction for learning and capability across your practice area, ensuring the organisation builds the skills it will need for the future.

• You act as a thought leader, holding a strong view of where your practice area is heading and shaping service provision towards it.

• You represent and shape the practice, bringing industry thinking and learning back into your practice.

• You create the conditions for others to lead development across their own areas, building a pipeline of expertise and next-generation leaders.

• You make clear decisions on where in your practice areas to invest in capability and where not to.

behaviours.name: Supporting and Developing Others
behaviours.def: How you support, develop and lead the people around you. Covers giving and receiving feedback, coaching and mentoring,  building autonomy and empowerment, and handling conflict.

levels.6: Graduate:
• You give constructive feedback to colleagues, thinking about how it will be received by the other person.

• You share what you're learning with colleagues and help colleagues with tasks you know how to complete.
levels.7: Junior:
• You give constructive feedback to colleagues, thinking about how it will be received by the other person.

• You share what you're learning with colleagues and help colleagues with tasks you know how to complete.
levels.8: Mid:
• You give clear, specific constructive feedback that helps those around you improve their approach to work.

• You are willing to give feedback upwards to more senior colleagues when it will help the work.
levels.9: Senior:
• You give colleagues the trust and space to deliver, stepping in where needed. 

• You recognise where others have individual strengths, and support and mentor them to engage meaningfully.

• You recognise when colleagues can benefit and learn from each other, and give them the encouragement to connect.

• You seek to understand how others are feeling and performing, and act to improve their situation.
levels.10: Lead:
• You build high-trust working environments, giving people the autonomy to deliver while staying close enough to unblock them.

• You mentor and coach those around you, and you give constructive feedback that recognises good work and helps people see their own progress.

• You identify sources of conflict early, bringing people together to surface and resolve issues openly so all parties feel heard before moving toward a resolution.

• You seek to understand the underlying needs of others, holding trust and maintaining positive relationships while still achieving the right outcome.
levels.11: Principal:
• You build high-trust working environments across engagements, ensuring colleagues have the clarity and support to deliver.

• You resolve conflict with empathy and directness, delivering difficult messages and bringing professional judgement to difficult situations.

• You develop others through structured discussions, clear frameworks, and honest difficult conversations.

• You remain pragmatic when colleagues face setbacks and keep them focused on what can move forward.

• You recognise when it is important to get involved in people issues, understand what's at stake if you don't, and default to stepping in when it counts.
levels.12: Head of:
• You model how people are developed and how feedback is given, maintaining clear standards across your practice and addressing performance gaps constructively and in a timely way.

• You handle the most complex people situations in your practice: organisational conflict, sensitive exits, and performance issues. You bring judgement and discretion to each.

• You build the leadership capability of those below you, developing the next generation of leaders to meet future needs of the practice.

• You demonstrate, encourage, and hold others accountable for the behaviours that create a culture of feedback, trust, and empowerment across your area.

behaviours.name: Communicating and Collaborating
behaviours.def: How you build trust through communication and collaboration. Covers adapting how you communicate for different audiences, working openly across peers and disciplines, navigating stakeholder dynamics, and advocating for others.

levels.6: Graduate:
• You communicate clearly with different audiences, adapting your language to suit who you are working with.

• You build working relationships with others based on curiosity, reliability, and respect.

• You build trust and credibility with peers by being reliable, contributing, and giving credit to others.

• You collaborate openly rather than working in isolation, ask for help when you need it, and follow the lead from senior colleagues on how you work with others.
levels.7: Junior:
• You communicate clearly with different audiences, adapting your language to suit who you are working with.

• You build working relationships with others based on curiosity, reliability, and respect.

• You build trust and credibility with peers by being reliable, contributing, and giving credit to others.

• You collaborate openly rather than working in isolation, ask for help when you need it, and follow the lead from senior colleagues on how you work with others.
levels.8: Mid:
• You tailor how you communicate with different stakeholders and clients, translating technical content into language that works for the audience.

• You build trust in client situations through building credibility by demonstrating expertise, being consistent, and delivering on your commitments.

• You collaborate across peers and disciplines, building your internal networks, knowing when to involve the right people, and recognising and acknowledging the value others contribute.

• You recognise when you hold a different perspective to a stakeholder and check in with senior colleagues on how to raise it and whether it is important to raise.
levels.9: Senior:
• You bridge between technical work and client understanding, creating a common understanding that aids communication in multidisciplinary settings.

• You build trust across the organisation and with clients through consistent delivery, clear communication, and a collaborative style.

• You work in the open, welcome other views, and make it easy for others to contribute, creating a sense of psychological safety in the groups you're part of.

• You identify where collaboration across disciplines would add value, exercising clear judgement on what to share, with whom, and at what moment, and you help colleagues understand what good looks like. 

• You recognise when stakeholders hold different perspectives to you, and discuss them to seek a solution, responding well to challenge in client sessions, delivering difficult messages with both honesty and a constructive tone.
levels.10: Lead:
• You frame and communicate work-related topics in ways that elevate its impact, connect delivery to the outcomes the client cares about.

• You build and sustain relationships across the organisation and with clients.

• You model supportive behaviour by welcoming other views, advocating for colleagues, and raising visibility of what they are achieving.

• You manage senior stakeholder relationships, knowing when to speak, when to hold back, and when to bring others into the conversation.

• You connect colleagues, clients, and leaders appropriately, so the right conversations happen at the right level.

• You recognise when stakeholders hold different perspectives and you facilitate the conversation that gets them to a shared view on how to move forward.
levels.11: Principal:
• You represent the organisation and your practice effectively, shaping perspectives through clear, memorable stories, communicating key messages and adjusting your narrative for different audiences and contexts.

• You represent your practice across the organisation and directly with clients, advocating for colleagues, and resetting boundaries without unnecessary escalation.

• You represent the organisation credibly through the decisions you make and how you communicate them, the relationships you hold, and the outcomes you shape.

• You set appropriate boundaries with clients, handle complex stakeholder dynamics, and build a network of trust across the organisation that your colleagues can access when needed.

• You handle situations where stakeholders' interests and priorities differ, bringing people together around a shared view.
levels.12: Head of:
• You represent the practice as a lead voice, shaping perspectives through narratives you adapt across audiences and contexts.

• You set the tone for how relationships are built and sustained across your practice area and with senior external stakeholders, creating a culture of safety and openness.

• You shape the strategic narrative of your practice area: how it is understood internally, discussed with clients externally, and connected to the organisation's wider direction.

• You lead the most challenging conversations, drawing on diverse inputs and signals to reset expectations, steer outcomes, and keep dynamics constructive without unnecessary escalation.

• You handle situations where senior stakeholders' interests and priorities differ, bringing people together around a shared view, whilst ensuring good quality relationships are maintained.

behaviours.name: Owning and delivering
behaviours.def: Taking responsibility for your work end-to-end and going beyond what was asked. Covers proactivity, adaptability and resourcefulness, managing scope and switching between contexts, spotting opportunities to add value

levels.6: Graduate:
• You contribute to specialist tasks by working with more senior colleagues, and ask for help when you need it.

• You manage your time and workload effectively, organising your diary and priorities, and consistently delivering to agreed deadlines and expected standards.

• When you identify issues in your work, you raise them with senior colleagues.

• You flag when you are at risk of missing a deadline early, keeping those affected informed.
levels.7: Junior:
• You contribute to specialist tasks by working with more senior colleagues, and ask for help when you need it.

• You manage your time and workload effectively, organising your diary and priorities, and consistently delivering to agreed deadlines and expected standards.

• When you identify issues in your work, you raise them with senior colleagues.

• You flag when you are at risk of missing a deadline early, keeping those affected informed.
levels.8: Mid:
• You own individual specialist tasks within your workstream. You take on more challenging work and ask for input when you need it.

• You understand how long elements of your work take, planning your work realistically.

• You manage your time and resources to make consistent progress, and communicate status updates so others can make informed decisions. 

• When you identify issues in your work, you ensure they are flagged or corrected before the project is complete.

• You context switch between tasks and contexts under guidance from colleagues, adjusting how you work when the client or project requires it.
levels.9: Senior:
• You support colleagues in areas where they have less familiarity, helping them get up to speed on the work.

• You recognise obstacles and blockers, mitigate the risks they create, and escalate the important ones to the relevant individuals.

• You spot opportunities to add value beyond the current scope, either through delivery or by feeding insights back to the relevant people.

• You accurately assess the time and effort a piece of work requires, and realistically evaluate your own capacity before committing.

• You manage your own energy and communicate how you best work, being able to switch contexts and maintain sustainable ways of operating.
levels.10: Lead:
• You lead by example in how tasks are planned and delivered, testing ideas to validate them and demonstrating value early.

• You model how to share what you're working on, your availability, and how you balance competing demands.

• You identify where you can add value beyond the current scope, and you model this for others.

• You respond to the needs of others and help to unblock the challenges they face, recognising when information needs to be escalated to senior colleagues.
levels.11: Principal:
• You reliably meet your commitments across all tasks and projects assigned to you, setting the example for how to plan, deliver, and review work to meet client expectations.

• You manage your time and energy across your work, maintaining consistent output without compromising your own effectiveness.

• You look ahead to anticipate challenges across your workload, and you address them before they become issues for your colleagues.

• You are alert to resource constraints, manage the risks they create, and know when to escalate these

• You switch credibly between client work, internal initiatives, and bids, holding multiple types of work with the ability to get back up to speed quickly on each of them.
levels.12: Head of:
• You hold your practice to a consistent standard for planning, delivery and quality, intervening visibly when work drifts and articulating what 'good' looks like.

• You define and communicate the principles, escalation paths and decision rights that govern how your practice operates, and ensure colleagues apply them consistently in their day-to-day work.

• You make clear decisions on scope and resource across the practice, naming the trade-offs between utilisation, development and delivery risks

• You anticipate resource constraints and act on them ahead of time, reallocating, renegotiating or escalating before it becomes a delivery risk.

behaviours.name: Navigating scope and complexity
behaviours.def: How you make sense of complexity, manage scope and shape direction. Covers strategic thinking, navigating ambiguity, connecting delivery decisions to broader outcomes, and managing scope change.

levels.6: Graduate:
• You stay curious about complexity and take interest in how things connect.

• You flag when information is unclear or incomplete, asking questions to clarify what you need before continuing.
levels.7: Junior:
• You stay curious about complexity and take interest in how things connect.

• You flag when information is unclear or incomplete, asking questions to clarify what you need before continuing.
levels.8: Mid:
• You keep making progress when it is not clear what you're working to resolve, identifying open questions rather than forcing premature answers.

• You work with the team to break ambiguous problems into smaller parts and make progress on what you can, asking for support when needed.

• You raise potential project scope creep early, renegotiating deadlines with project leads when appropriate.

• You identify patterns across your work, recognising when a challenge you've seen before is appearing in a new context, and you apply what you've learned.

• You understand how your work connects to the broader project or programme goals.
levels.9: Senior:
• You work through ambiguous problems by structuring them, laying out options, trade-offs, and a recommended path with incomplete information.

• You spot issues early and escalate them in time for others to act, and you help teammates work through their own escalations.

• You understand what good outcomes look like at the end of the engagement, connecting delivery decisions back to the client's wider outcomes.

• You make sound decisions under pressure with incomplete information.

• You set boundaries and prioritise with judgement, knowing what's in scope, what isn't, and what to say no to.

• You support colleagues through specialist tasks, helping them see how their work ties to wider project and organisational objectives.
levels.10: Lead:
• You remain composed when an engagement becomes complex or unclear, bringing clarity and structure by committing to a path with incomplete information and adjusting as more becomes clear.

• You connect delivery decisions to the broader outcomes of the engagement, articulating how each decision contributes to achieving the client's goals.

• You set boundaries that are realistic to deliver against, and manage the scope of the engagement in spite of pressure to change it.

• You shape scope on engagements and protect the focus of those delivering, declining low-value requests and absorbing the ones that matter.

• You support others in discussions around negotiating trade-offs with the client openly, having open dialogue about what would need to be compromised if something new is added or changed.
levels.11: Principal:
• You hold complexity across your work, tracing cause and effect, triaging incoming information, and managing risk.

• You set strategic direction in ambiguous situations, clarifying ill-defined or complex problems and making decisions so that work can progress

• You connect delivery decisions to the client's strategic and commercial outcomes, ensuring choices made serve the broader value the client is seeking.

• You make sound decisions when information is incomplete and a decision is needed, and colleagues seek you out for your judgement in high-stakes situations.

• You make the decisions on how scope is shaped across the projects you oversee, balancing the client's request with what can realistically be delivered well.

• You shield colleagues from organisational noise so they can focus on the work that matters.
levels.12: Head of:
• You make high-stakes decisions where information is incomplete and the stakes are significant, and you stand behind those decisions.

• You define the approach the practice takes to understand the opportunities and challenges a certain engagement presents, informing the ultimate approach taken.

• You give others clear visibility of your team's priorities and strategic direction, and make course corrections to colleagues' approaches as needed.

• You identify how current challenges and opportunities can unlock value for your practice area, and you act to meet them, through capability, resourcing, or commercial moves.
